title: The Lid Situation
angle: The mismatch between food containers and their lids turns a kitchen cupboard into a comic lesson in the limits of neat categories.
paragraphs: Some kitchen cupboards contain a small constitutional crisis: the food containers are stacked together, while their lids occupy a separate and apparently sovereign territory. A rectangular lid appears; no known rectangle claims it. One round tub fits perfectly, but only after its matching lid has been promoted to an entirely different shelf.

The cupboard has clearly attempted a system. Containers nest inside one another, lids lean upright, and a few pieces wait in the uncertain middle ground where neither group will accept them. This is not quite disorder. It is more like two departments maintaining immaculate records that do not communicate.

A lid can look promising from across the drawer, then reveal a crucial difference in diameter. The container beneath it may belong to a set that has long since vanished from the household, perhaps carried away by a lunch that never returned. No one can prove this, but the theory has the useful quality of explaining nothing.

Eventually, a container gets a lid that is almost right, and the cupboard closes. The arrangement remains less a solved puzzle than a diplomatic agreement: imperfect, temporary, and good enough to keep leftovers in the fridge.
